cards.front: In order, what five parts does a nervous response route run through, from stimulus to response?
cards.back: Receptor, sensory neuron, integrating centre (spinal cord or brain), motor neuron, effector (the muscle or gland that responds).
cards.quote: A nervous response runs a route: receptor (which detects the change), sensory neuron, integrating centre

cards.front: In the simple chain-of-neurons model, what three kinds of terms add up to a reflex's response time?
cards.back: Axon time (each axon's length over its conduction velocity, L/v, added up), synapses in the cord × about 1 ms each, and end delays at the receptor, the nerve-muscle junction and the muscle.
cards.quote: Its time is the sum of its legs: each axon's length over its speed, about a millisecond per synapse in the cord, and short delays at the ends

cards.front: In the reflex-timing model, why can a central delay suggest a synapse count but not prove it?
cards.back: The 1 ms per synapse is a teaching assumption. Real synapses and cord processing vary and often take longer, so the count is an inference that anatomy or other recordings must confirm.
cards.quote: real synapses and cord processing vary and often take longer, so a delay suggests a synapse count but cannot prove it

cards.front: A timing sum can predict when a heart's response to a nerve signal begins. Why can it not predict whether the heart speeds up or slows down?
cards.back: Direction depends on which autonomic division reaches the heart, the transmitter it releases, and the receptor that transmitter acts on. None of these enters the timing sum.
cards.quote: whether the heart speeds up or slows down depends on which division reaches it, its transmitter and the receptor that transmitter acts on

cards.front: Name a neuron's four main parts and the job of each.
cards.back: Dendrites take in signals; the cell body (soma) holds the nucleus; the axon carries the signal away; axon terminals pass it on to the next cell.
cards.quote: dendrites take in signals, the cell body (soma) holds the nucleus, one axon carries the signal away
cards.section: One neuron: what the first film left out

cards.front: An action potential is {{c1::all-or-none}}: full size past a threshold, none below it.
cards.quote: it is all-or-none: full size past a threshold, none below it
cards.section: One neuron: what the first film left out

cards.front: Under the all-or-none rule, how can a neuron signal that one stimulus is stronger than another?
cards.back: It fires more often, and a stronger stimulus can bring more neurons into action. It cannot make an individual impulse taller.
cards.quote: So a stronger stimulus makes the neuron fire more often, and can bring more neurons into action, but cannot make an impulse taller.
cards.section: One neuron: what the first film left out

cards.front: At most synapses, how does a signal cross from one cell to the next?
cards.back: The cells do not touch: a released neurotransmitter crosses a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft. Some synapses are instead electrical, with ions passing straight between cells.
cards.quote: At most synapses the cells do not touch: a neurotransmitter crosses a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft.
cards.section: One neuron: what the first film left out

cards.front: Which glial cells make myelin outside the brain and spinal cord, and which make it inside?
cards.back: Schwann cells outside the brain and spinal cord; oligodendrocytes inside.
cards.quote: Schwann cells outside the brain and spinal cord, oligodendrocytes inside
cards.section: One neuron: what the first film left out

cards.front: In the two-point method, conduction velocity v = {{c1::difference in distance / difference in time}}.
cards.quote: conduction velocity v = difference in distance / difference in time
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: In two-point timing of a frog nerve, why divide the difference in distance by the difference in delay, rather than one distance by one whole delay?
cards.back: Both trials share the same junction and muscle delay. Subtracting one trial from the other cancels it, leaving only the extra nerve time, so the result is the true speed whatever the shared delay.
cards.quote: The difference between two trials gives 25 m per s whatever the shared delay.
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: An illustrative frog nerve has a true conduction velocity of 30 m per s. It is stimulated 60 mm from the muscle, and the junction and muscle add 2 ms. What speed would you report if you divided whole length by whole delay?
cards.back: Nerve time = 0.060 m / 30 m per s = 2.0 ms, so the whole delay is 4.0 ms. 0.060 m / 0.0040 s = 15 m per s, half the true speed, because the shared end delay is counted as nerve time.
cards.quote: Had Helmholtz skipped the subtraction and divided whole length by whole delay
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: Two stimulus points on a frog nerve are 45 mm apart. Contraction starts 1.8 ms later from the far point than from the near one. What is the conduction velocity?
cards.back: v = difference in distance / difference in time = 0.045 m / 0.0018 s = 25 m per s.
cards.quote: Two stimulus points on a frog nerve are 30 mm apart.
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: Two-point timing of a frog nerve at room temperature gives 25 m per s. Predict the result if the same nerve is cooled, and say whether either value can stand in for a human nerve at 37 °C.
cards.back: The estimate falls, because cooling slows conduction in a given fibre. Neither is a human value: a frog is an ectotherm, whose body temperature follows its surroundings.
cards.quote: cooling slows conduction in a given fibre, so a room-temperature frog value is not a human value at 37 °C
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: Knee-jerk model: sensory and motor axons each 0.5 m at 60 m per s, one synapse of 1.0 ms, and 1.5 ms at the junction and muscle. Estimate the latency.
cards.back: Each axon: 0.5 / 60 = 0.0083 s = 8.3 ms. 8.3 + 8.3 + 1.0 + 1.5 = about 19 ms, close to the measured adult latency of about 20 ms.
cards.why: The sum leaves out the short time from tap to spindle firing, so the near match is not a full accounting.
cards.quote: The film's sensory and motor axons are each about 0.5 m at 60 m per s
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: In the knee-jerk model (two 0.5 m axons, one synapse of about 1 ms), suppose both axons conducted at 5 m per s instead of 60 m per s. How long would axons plus synapse take, and which term dominates?
cards.back: 0.5 / 5 = 0.1 s = 100 ms per axon; 100 + 100 + 1 = 201 ms, versus 17.7 ms at 60 m per s, about 11 times longer. Axon time dominates.
cards.quote: In this model axon time is the large term
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: Why does a wider axon conduct an impulse faster?
cards.back: A wider axon offers less resistance to the current spreading ahead of the impulse, so the impulse travels faster.
cards.quote: a wider axon offers less resistance to the current spreading ahead of the impulse, so the impulse travels faster
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: How does myelin speed conduction along a vertebrate axon?
cards.back: The impulse is renewed only at the nodes of Ranvier, the bare gaps in the myelin, not along every bit of membrane, so it skips ahead.
cards.quote: the impulse is renewed only at the nodes, not along every bit of membrane, so it skips ahead
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: The squid's unmyelinated giant axon is about half a millimetre across and conducts at roughly 20 m per s; the largest myelinated vertebrate motor axons are about 20 micrometres across and conduct faster. What advantage does myelin give a vertebrate nerve?
cards.back: Myelin buys speed without width, so a vertebrate fits many fast axons into one nerve.
cards.quote: Myelin buys speed without width, so a vertebrate fits many fast axons into one nerve.
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: Suppose a vertebrate's knee-jerk sensory and motor axons lost their myelin but still conducted, renewing the impulse along every bit of membrane. Predict the effect on the reflex latency and on its central delay.
cards.back: Latency rises sharply; the central delay stays about the same. Axon conduction slows without node-to-node skipping, axon time is the large term, and the single cord synapse is unchanged.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: myelin speeds conduction, and response time = axon L/v terms + synapses × about 1 ms + end delays.
cards.quote: In this model axon time is the large term, and two main features of the axon set its speed
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: What makes up the central nervous system (CNS), and what makes up the peripheral nervous system (PNS)?
cards.back: CNS: the brain and spinal cord. PNS: everything outside, the nerves and ganglia (clusters of nerve cell bodies).
cards.quote: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything outside: nerves and ganglia, clusters of nerve cell bodies.
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: Which effectors does the somatic division of the PNS drive, and which does the autonomic division drive?
cards.back: Somatic: skeletal muscle. Autonomic: cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
cards.quote: Its somatic division drives skeletal muscle; its autonomic division drives cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: In bright light the pupil narrows automatically, with no decision by the person. Does the motor path belong to the somatic or the autonomic division, and why?
cards.back: Autonomic. The division is set by the effector, not by whether a decision is involved: the pupil is narrowed by smooth muscle of the iris. The knee jerk, also automatic, is somatic because its effector is skeletal muscle.
cards.quote: its autonomic division drives cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: In the knee jerk, how does a tap on the tendon below the kneecap start the sensory signal?
cards.back: The tap stretches the quadriceps through its tendon, so its muscle spindles (stretch receptors) fire through large, fast sensory fibres called Ia fibres.
cards.quote: the tap stretches the quadriceps through its tendon, so its muscle spindles, stretch receptors, fire through large, fast sensory fibres called Ia fibres
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: Contrast the spinal cord wiring of the knee-jerk reflex with that of the withdrawal reflex.
cards.back: The knee jerk's direct excitatory path is monosynaptic, sensory neuron straight to motor neuron (its hamstring branch uses an interneuron, a neuron wholly within the CNS). The withdrawal reflex uses interneurons from the start.
cards.quote: in the knee jerk only the direct excitatory path lacks one, and the withdrawal reflex uses them from the start
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: In the withdrawal reflex, what is reciprocal innervation?
cards.back: The pairing of excited flexor muscles with inhibited extensor muscles.
cards.quote: called its pairing of excited flexors and inhibited extensors reciprocal innervation
cards.section: The reflex arc: what the second film left out

cards.front: Withdrawal-reflex model: a 0.9 m pain fibre at 20 m per s, three synapses in the cord at about 1 ms each, a 0.9 m motor axon at 60 m per s, and 1.5 ms at the junction and muscle. Estimate the latency.
cards.back: Sensory 0.9 / 20 = 45 ms; motor 0.9 / 60 = 15 ms; 45 + 3 + 15 + 1.5 = 64.5, about 65 ms. Measured human withdrawal responses are usually slower, near a tenth of a second.
cards.quote: the withdrawal's thin pain fibre runs from the sole, its motor axon to a flexor lower in the leg
cards.section: Counting synapses with a clock

cards.front: The knee-jerk model takes about 19 ms and the withdrawal model about 65 ms, with the same end delays. Does the withdrawal lose its extra time mainly on axons or at synapses? Show the split.
cards.back: Axons. Sensory adds 45 - 8.3 = 36.7 ms and motor adds 15 - 8.3 = 6.7 ms, about 43 ms in all; the two extra synapses add only about 2 ms.
cards.why: Rests on the sum of axon L/v terms, synapses × about 1 ms, and end delays: the long, slow pain fibre is the big term.
cards.quote: does the slower one lose its time on axons or at synapses?
cards.section: How fast? What Helmholtz's subtraction can tell you

cards.front: A stretch reflex has a latency of 25 ms. Calculated axon conduction time is 20 ms, and the delays at receptor, junction and muscle total 4 ms. Assuming about 1 ms per synapse, estimate the central delay and the number of synapses in series.
cards.back: Central delay = 25 - 20 - 4 = 1 ms, which fits one synapse, a direct sensory-to-motor connection. This is an inference, not a count.
cards.quote: near 1 ms fits one synapse and near 3 ms about three in series
cards.section: Counting synapses with a clock

cards.front: In the withdrawal model (pain fibre truly 0.9 m at 20 m per s, three synapses), an experimenter wrongly assumes the pain fibre conducts at 60 m per s. What central delay will they calculate, and what synapse count will it suggest?
cards.back: Assumed sensory time is 0.9 / 60 = 15 ms instead of 45 ms, so 30 ms of axon time stays in the central delay: 3 + 30 = 33 ms, suggesting about 33 synapses instead of 3.
cards.why: Central delay = latency minus axon time and end delays, so a slow fibre's speed set too high turns its extra time into apparent synapses.
cards.quote: set a slow fibre's speed too high and its extra time looks like extra synapses
cards.section: Counting synapses with a clock

cards.front: Timing alone gives a withdrawal reflex a central delay near 3 ms. What further evidence would you need before concluding that its path has three synapses in series?
cards.back: Measure the axons' actual conduction speeds, so slow fibre time is not mistaken for synapse time, and confirm the count with anatomy or other recordings, since real synapses and cord processing can take longer than 1 ms.
cards.quote: an inference, not a count, which anatomy or other recordings must confirm
cards.section: Counting synapses with a clock

cards.front: In an autonomic motor path to the heart, gut or glands, which two neurons usually run in series, and where does each sit?
cards.back: A preganglionic neuron in the CNS, then a postganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in a peripheral ganglion and whose axon reaches the organ.
cards.quote: a preganglionic neuron in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron whose cell body sits in a peripheral ganglion
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: In humans, from which parts of the CNS do the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions leave?
cards.back: Sympathetic: thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord (thoracolumbar). Parasympathetic: the brainstem, in cranial nerves such as the vagus, and the sacral cord (craniosacral).
cards.quote: The parasympathetic division leaves from the brainstem, in cranial nerves such as the vagus, and from the sacral cord (craniosacral).
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: In humans, what do the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions each do to heart rate, the pupil and gut peristalsis?
cards.back: Sympathetic: raises heart rate, dilates the pupil, inhibits peristalsis. Parasympathetic: lowers heart rate, constricts the pupil, promotes peristalsis and digestion.
cards.quote: The divisions oppose each other at the heart, the iris and the gut, but not everywhere.
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: Where in humans do the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions not oppose each other, and how is control exerted there?
cards.back: Most blood vessels and the eccrine sweat glands have only a sympathetic supply, turned up or down. The sympathetic fibres to sweat glands release acetylcholine, not norepinephrine.
cards.quote: Most vessels and the sweat glands have only a sympathetic supply, turned up or down.
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: In the rabbit parotid salivary gland, how did sympathetic stimulation interact with parasympathetic secretion?
cards.back: It increased flow on top of a parasympathetic background secretion, so there the two divisions worked in the same direction.
cards.quote: In the rabbit parotid salivary gland, sympathetic stimulation increased flow on top of a parasympathetic background secretion
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: A drug that blocks the sympathetic effect on the radial (dilator) muscle of the iris is dropped into one eye in normal light. Predict the treated pupil's size relative to the other eye, and why.
cards.back: Narrower. Sympathetic input dilates the pupil through the radial muscle; with it blocked, parasympathetic input to the circular muscle constricts the pupil unopposed.
cards.quote: The divisions oppose each other at the heart, the iris and the gut
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: A drug blocks acetylcholine's action at autonomic target organs but leaves norepinephrine's action intact. Predict the effect on sweating from human eccrine sweat glands, and why.
cards.back: Sweating falls. Eccrine sweat glands have only a sympathetic supply, and those sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine, an exception to the usual sympathetic transmitter, norepinephrine.
cards.quote: Most vessels and the sweat glands have only a sympathetic supply
cards.section: Two autonomic divisions and their exceptions

cards.front: In a drug-blockade study of the heart, what is the pacemaker's intrinsic rate, and how is it revealed?
cards.back: The rate with no autonomic input. It is revealed by blocking both divisions at once: atropine for the parasympathetic effect plus propranolol for the sympathetic effect through beta receptors.
cards.quote: With both divisions blocked, the pacemaker runs at its intrinsic rate, the rate with no autonomic input
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Illustrative blockade data, healthy adults at rest: heart rate 80 beats per minute; after atropine 115; after propranolol 72; after both drugs 105. Which division dominates the resting rate, and how large is each effect?
cards.back: Intrinsic rate is 105. Rest is 25 below it, so the net effect is braking. Propranolol leaves only parasympathetic input: 72, so vagal braking is 33. Atropine leaves only sympathetic input: 115, so sympathetic drive adds 10. Parasympathetic dominates.
cards.quote: So at rest the parasympathetic division dominates, and sympathetic drive adds a little.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Blockade data: resting heart rate 70; after atropine 110; after propranolol 62; after both 100. The separate effects, vagal -38 and sympathetic +10, sum to -28, but the observed net effect is -30. What does the mismatch mean, and what must hold for the analysis to be valid?
cards.back: The two divisions do not combine as simple addition. And the conclusion holds only if each drug fully blocks its own division, and nothing else, at the dose used.
cards.quote: One check: the conclusion holds only if each drug fully blocks its own division, and nothing else, at the dose used.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How is the nervous system of Hydra, a freshwater cnidarian, laid out?
cards.back: As a nerve net: neurons spread through the body wall and connected in a mesh, with no brain and no separate integrating centre.
cards.why: It is a working nervous system in a living lineage, not an unfinished brain.
cards.quote: Hydra, a freshwater cnidarian, has a nerve net: neurons spread through the body wall and connected in a mesh, with no brain.
cards.section: Four layouts of neurons

cards.front: Compare the main nerve cords of a planarian, an earthworm and a vertebrate in position and structure.
cards.back: Planarian: two ventral cords joined like ladder rungs, a head ganglion. Earthworm: one ventral cord, a ganglion per segment. Vertebrate: a dorsal hollow cord (spinal cord) with a brain in front. The planarian and earthworm cords are solid.
cards.quote: Vertebrates, such as a frog or a human, have a dorsal hollow nerve cord, the spinal cord, running along the back
cards.section: Four layouts of neurons
